e-74.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
e-74.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{x-2\sqrt{x}}{x-4} & =\frac{4-2\sqrt{4}}{4-4}=\frac{0}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\eqalign{
	\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x - 2\sqrt{x}} {x - 4} &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {(x -2 \sqrt{x})(x+2\sqrt x)} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
            &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x^2-\left(2\sqrt{x}\right)^2} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x^2-4x} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x(x-4)} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x} {x+2\sqrt x} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {4} {4+2\sqrt4} \
	    &=\dfrac 1 2.
	}
$$

e-75.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
e-75.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{3x}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} & =\frac{3\cdot 0}{\sqrt{0+1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac {3x} {\sqrt{x + 1} - 1} 
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{(3x)(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{x + 1} - 1)(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{\left(\sqrt{x+1}\right)^2-1^2}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{x+1-1}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{x}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}3(\sqrt{x+1}+1)\
&=3(\sqrt{0+1}+1)\
	&=6.
}
$$

decision.explanation: Factor the numerator as √x(√x−8) and the denominator as (√x−8)(√x+8). Canceling gives √x/(√x+8), which approaches 8/(8+8)=1/2 as x approaches 64 from the left.

after.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (64)^{-}}\frac{x-8\sqrt{x}}{x-64} & =\frac{64-8\sqrt{64}}{64-64}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (64)^{-}}\frac{x-8\sqrt{x}}{x-64} & ={lim}_{x\to (64)^{-}}\frac{(x-8\sqrt{x})(x+8\sqrt{x})}{(x-64)(x+8\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (64)^{-}}\frac{{x}^{2}-{(8\sqrt{x})}^{2}}{(x-64)(x+8\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (64)^{-}}\frac{{x}^{2}-64x}{(x-64)(x+8\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (64)^{-}}\frac{x(x-64)}{(x-64)(x+8\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (64)^{-}}\frac{x}{x+8\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{64}{64+8\sqrt{64}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{{x}^{2}-4} & =\frac{\sqrt{2+2}-2}{{2}^{2}-4}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{(x-2)(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{x+2}-2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{{(\sqrt{x+2})}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x+2-4}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x-2}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(2+2)(\sqrt{2+2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{{x}^{2}-4} & =\frac{\sqrt{2+2}-2}{{2}^{2}-4}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{(x-2)(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{x+2}-2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{{(\sqrt{x+2})}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x+2-4}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x-2}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(2+2)(\sqrt{2+2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$
